pieces.au: The essays were signed "Brutus." Many historians have attributed them to Robert Yates, a New York judge who left the Constitutional Convention early in protest, but there is no direct proof. Others have suggested Melancton Smith or John Williams. The author is not known for certain.
pieces.desc: A guide to the sixteen essays of Brutus, the strongest Anti-Federalist series: what each one argues, the Federalist papers that answer them, and where to read the full texts.
pieces.c: Brutus wrote to the citizens of New York in the New-York Journal, starting three weeks after the Constitution was published and a week before the first Federalist paper. Many scholars consider Brutus the ablest Anti-Federalist writer. Hamilton answered him directly in the judiciary papers (Nos. 78 to 83), and Brutus's warning about the courts is still discussed in debates about judicial review.
pieces.m: Brutus argues that the Constitution would create one consolidated national government, not a federation, because its powers to tax, to make all "necessary and proper" laws, and to establish courts whose decisions are supreme would leave the states little to do. A free republic, he says, cannot work over so large and varied a country; representatives would be too few and too far from the people, and laws would have to be enforced by soldiers. He calls for a bill of rights, limits on peacetime armies, and a judiciary that answers to someone.
qs: Brutus says a free republic cannot extend over a large territory. Compare his reasons with Madison's answer in Federalist 10.

Brutus warned that federal judges, interpreting the Constitution by its "spirit," would be above any control. Read Federalist 78 and 81. Who has the stronger argument? Has history settled the question?
Which of Brutus's fears were answered by the Bill of Rights, and which were not?
also: Read the full texts: [Brutus I at the National Constitution Center](https://constitutioncenter.org/the-constitution/historic-document-library/detail/brutus-essay-no-1) and [all sixteen essays at Teaching American History](https://teachingamericanhistory.org/resource/fafd-home/fafd-selected-antifederalist-collections/fafd-brutus-letters-from-the-federalist-antifederalist-debates).
The Historical Society of the New York Courts lists the Brutus essays by date in [The Anti-Federalist Papers](https://history.nycourts.gov/about_period/antifederalist-papers/).
A Federalist reply from 1787: Pelatiah Webster, *The Weakness of Brutus Exposed*, in Ford's *Pamphlets on the Constitution* (1888).
pieces.summ:
**Why there is no full text here.** We could not reach a public-domain printing of the Brutus essays from the libraries we use, so this page gives a careful summary of each essay and links to full texts elsewhere. Read them there; they are worth it.

| No. | Date (1787–88) | What Brutus argues |
|---|---|---|
| I | Oct. 18 | The plan would merge the states into one government. Its powers to tax, to make all "necessary and proper" laws, and its supreme courts would leave the states nothing. A free republic cannot cover a country this large and varied. |
| II | Nov. 1 | A bill of rights is needed. People give up some natural rights to form a government, so the rights they keep must be written down. The Constitution's own short list of protections (habeas corpus, no ex post facto laws) shows such lists matter. |
| III | Nov. 15 | Representation is badly arranged: the rule counting three-fifths of enslaved people adds to some states' seats, and equal votes in the Senate are unfair to large states. |
| IV | Nov. 29 | The House is too small to know or reflect the people, and too small to resist bribery. Congress's power over elections could be abused. |
| V | Dec. 13 | The taxing power, read with the General Welfare and Necessary and Proper clauses, has no real limit. |
| VI | Dec. 27 | Unlimited federal taxing power would leave the states without revenue and so without real power. |
| VII | Jan. 3 | More on taxes: the nation's needs do not require power over every source of revenue, and the states need sources of their own. |
| VIII | Jan. 10 | The powers to borrow money and to raise armies without limit are dangerous. |
| IX | Jan. 17 | Standing armies in peacetime have destroyed liberty in other countries. |
| X | Jan. 24 | More on armies: history from Rome to Cromwell. Peacetime armies should need a two-thirds vote of Congress. |
| XI | Jan. 31 | The federal courts will read the Constitution by its "spirit" and steadily enlarge federal power. |
| XII | Feb. 7 and 14 | More on how the courts' reasoning will extend national power over the states. |
| XIII | Feb. 21 | States should not be sued in federal court by individuals. |
| XIV | Feb. 28 and Mar. 6 | Appeals "both as to law and fact" endanger trial by jury and burden people with distant courts. |
| XV | Mar. 20 | Judges serving for life, whose rulings no one can correct, would be independent of the people and above the legislature. |
| XVI | Apr. 10 | The Senate's six-year terms, its share in executive power and the lack of rotation or recall are dangerous. |

Dates follow the list kept by the Historical Society of the New York Courts, except Brutus II, which is not on that list and appeared on November 1, 1787. Summaries are our own.

pieces.au: Signed "Cato." Writers of the day, and Ford's 1892 edition used here, credited George Clinton, New York's governor. Some modern historians doubt this and have suggested other New York Anti-Federalists, such as Abraham Yates Jr. The author is not known for certain.
pieces.desc: Cato I (September 27, 1787): the full text with paragraph numbers, a short introduction, key passages and the Federalist reply.
pieces.c: Cato wrote to the citizens of New York just ten days after the Constitutional Convention adjourned, before most people had studied the plan. This first letter is short and calm.
pieces.m: Cato asks readers to take their time, to read the plan carefully and judge it for themselves, and not to accept it because famous men support it. He promises to examine the plan in later letters.

k.q: Deliberate, therefore, on this new national government with coolness; analize it with criticism; and reflect on it with candor
k.w: Cato's advice to readers.

k.q: Beware of those who wish to influence your passions
k.w: A warning both sides gave each other.

qs: Why does Cato warn against trusting the plan because of the reputation of its authors? Compare Jay's argument in Federalist 2.
What does Cato ask his readers to do before deciding?

pieces.au: Signed "Cato." Writers of the day, and Ford's 1892 edition used here, credited George Clinton, New York's governor. Some modern historians doubt this and have suggested other New York Anti-Federalists, such as Abraham Yates Jr. The author is not known for certain.
pieces.desc: Cato II (October 11, 1787): the full text with paragraph numbers, a short introduction, key passages and the Federalist reply.
pieces.c: Cato replies to "Caesar," a writer who had scolded him for questioning the Convention. Ford, whose edition is used here, believed Caesar was Hamilton, but that is uncertain.
pieces.m: Cato defends the right of free citizens to discuss the plan. In a republic, power comes from the people, and they have every right to examine a new frame of government before accepting it.

k.q: In democratic republics the people collectively are considered as the sovereign
k.w: Cato's view of where power comes from.

qs: Why does Cato say citizens have a right to debate the Constitution?
Is it ever wise to discourage public debate on a new law? What would Cato say?

pieces.au: Signed "Cato." Writers of the day, and Ford's 1892 edition used here, credited George Clinton, New York's governor. Some modern historians doubt this and have suggested other New York Anti-Federalists, such as Abraham Yates Jr. The author is not known for certain.
pieces.desc: Cato III (October 25, 1787): the full text with paragraph numbers, a short introduction, key passages and the Federalist reply.
pieces.c: Cato now begins his argument against the plan, starting with the size of the country.
pieces.m: Cato argues, citing Montesquieu, that a republic must be small enough for people to know and trust their government. The United States is too large and too varied in climate, economy and customs for one government to rule fairly; it would need force to keep order.

k.q: like a pebble cast on the calm surface of a river
k.w: His image of how loyalty fades with distance.

k.q: The strongest principle of union resides within our domestic walls
k.w: Cato's image of loyalty spreading out from the home.

qs: Why does Cato think a large republic would need force to govern?
Compare Cato's pebble image with Hamilton's argument in Federalist 17 that loyalty stays close to home. They agree on the fact but draw different conclusions. How?
How does Madison's Federalist 10 answer Cato?

pieces.au: Signed "Cato." Writers of the day, and Ford's 1892 edition used here, credited George Clinton, New York's governor. Some modern historians doubt this and have suggested other New York Anti-Federalists, such as Abraham Yates Jr. The author is not known for certain.
pieces.desc: Cato IV (November 8, 1787): the full text with paragraph numbers, a short introduction, key passages and the Federalist reply.
pieces.c: Cato turns to the presidency.
pieces.m: Cato argues that the President's powers are too great and his term too long, with no limit on re-election. He has no council, could build a court of flatterers in the capital, and commands the army. The Vice President is unnecessary and blends executive and legislative roles.

k.q: in all magistracies, the greatness of the power must be compensated by the brevity of the duration
k.w: Cato quotes Montesquieu.

k.q: The establishment of a vice-president is as unnecessary as it is dangerous
k.w: His objection to the Vice President.

qs: What is Cato's main fear about the President?
Read Federalist 69. How does Hamilton answer the comparison between the President and a king?
Why did some Anti-Federalists want a council to advise the President?

pieces.au: Signed "Cato." Writers of the day, and Ford's 1892 edition used here, credited George Clinton, New York's governor. Some modern historians doubt this and have suggested other New York Anti-Federalists, such as Abraham Yates Jr. The author is not known for certain.
pieces.desc: Cato V (November 22, 1787): the full text with paragraph numbers, a short introduction, key passages and the Federalist reply.
pieces.c: Cato continues on the executive and turns to the House of Representatives.
pieces.m: Cato says the Constitution's language is vague in dangerous places. He argues that the House is too small, its terms too long, and its members too few to resist corruption or to know the people's needs.

k.q: It is a very important objection to this government, that the representation consists of so few
k.w: His complaint about the House.

qs: Why does Cato think a larger House would be safer?
Compare Federalist 55's answer about the size of the House.

pieces.au: Signed "Cato." Writers of the day, and Ford's 1892 edition used here, credited George Clinton, New York's governor. Some modern historians doubt this and have suggested other New York Anti-Federalists, such as Abraham Yates Jr. The author is not known for certain.
pieces.desc: Cato VI (December 13, 1787): the full text with paragraph numbers, a short introduction, key passages and the Federalist reply.
pieces.c: Cato addresses how representatives and direct taxes are divided among the states, and the risk of an aristocracy.
pieces.m: Cato argues that apportioning representatives and direct taxes by the same population count is unjust, and objects to the federal taxing power. He warns that the Senate and President, linked together, could form an aristocracy.

k.q: The next objection that arises against this proffered constitution is, that the apportionment of representatives and direct taxes are unjust
k.w: His opening objection.

k.q: In every civilized community, even in those of the most democratic kind, there are principles which lead to an aristocracy
k.w: His warning about aristocracy.

qs: What is Cato's objection to how taxes and representatives are apportioned?
Compare Federalist 54 on the same clause.

pieces.au: Signed "Cato." Writers of the day, and Ford's 1892 edition used here, credited George Clinton, New York's governor. Some modern historians doubt this and have suggested other New York Anti-Federalists, such as Abraham Yates Jr. The author is not known for certain.
pieces.desc: Cato VII (January 3, 1788): the full text with paragraph numbers, a short introduction, key passages and the Federalist reply.
pieces.c: This is the last of Cato's letters. Ford notes that the New York legislature met a few days later.
pieces.m: Cato says the President and Senate are too closely connected to check each other. He objects strongly to Congress's power to regulate the times, places and manner of elections, which he thinks could be used to keep the people from voting freely.

k.q: That the president and senate are further improperly connected
k.w: His point about the Senate and President.

k.q: Among the many evils that are incorporated in this new system of government is that of congress having the power of making or altering the regulations
k.w: The election power, which Hamilton defends in Federalist 59 to 61.

qs: Why does Cato object to Congress's power over elections?
Read Federalist 59. Which side makes the stronger case, and why?

pieces.au: Signed "Centinel." Generally attributed to Samuel Bryan of Philadelphia, son of the judge and politician George Bryan; some people at the time suspected George Bryan himself. Most historians accept Samuel Bryan as the author.
pieces.desc: Centinel I (October 5, 1787), the first major Anti-Federalist essay: the full text, an introduction, key passages and the Federalist reply.
pieces.c: Pennsylvania moved quickly to ratify, and Centinel wrote in Philadelphia less than three weeks after the Convention closed. Pennsylvania's own 1776 constitution had a single-house legislature and a weak executive, which Centinel admired. He wrote many more letters (Centinel I to XVIII appeared in 1787–88).
pieces.m: Centinel defends the rights in Pennsylvania's constitution: freedom from general warrants, jury trial and a free press. He argues that the best government is a simple one, where the people can see who is responsible, and attacks John Adams's theory of balanced orders. The proposed plan, he says, gives Congress unlimited taxing power and supreme laws and courts, would absorb the states, and would become "a permanent aristocracy." It has no bill of rights and no protection for the press or civil juries. He also suggests that Washington and Franklin had been used by the plan's backers.

k.q: whether your houses shall continue to be your castles
k.w: The rights Centinel says are at stake.

k.q: the highest responsibility is to be attained in a simple structure of government
k.w: His theory of government, opposite to Madison's.

k.q: it would be in practice a permanent aristocracy
k.w: His conclusion about the plan.

k.q: that grand palladium of freedom, and scourge of tyrants
k.w: His words on the free press.

qs: Why does Centinel prefer a simple government with one legislature? Compare Madison in Federalist 47 to 51.
What rights in Pennsylvania's constitution does Centinel say are threatened? Which later appear in the Bill of Rights?
Centinel suggests that Washington and Franklin were misled. Is this fair argument or a personal attack? How does Federalist 1 discuss attacks on motives?

pieces.t: Letters from the Federal Farmer, I
pieces.au: Signed "The Federal Farmer." For about two centuries the letters were credited to Richard Henry Lee of Virginia, as in Ford's edition used here. Many modern scholars doubt this. Some have argued for Melancton Smith of New York, and more recently some have argued for Elbridge Gerry. The author is still debated.
pieces.desc: Federal Farmer I (dated October 8, 1787): the full text with paragraph numbers, an introduction, key passages and the Federalist reply.
pieces.c: The Federal Farmer's letters, addressed to "the Republican," were printed as a pamphlet in New York late in 1787 and sold widely. They are often praised as the most balanced Anti-Federalist writing. The writer says he wants a stronger federal government, but not this one.
pieces.m: The writer says there is no emergency that requires a hasty decision. The plan is partly federal but aims at one consolidated government. He describes three possible forms: separate states in a loose league, complete consolidation, or partial consolidation. Only partial consolidation, with real but limited federal powers and strong states, can keep both union and liberty in a country this large.

k.q: A federal government of some sort is necessary
k.w: He grants the need for change.

k.q: The plan proposed appears to be partly federal, but principally however, calculated ultimately to make the states one consolidated government
k.w: Compare Madison's "partly national, partly federal" in Federalist 39.

k.q: The third plan, or partial consolidation, is, in my opinion, the only one that can secure the freedom and happiness of this people
k.w: His preferred middle path.

qs: What are the three plans the Federal Farmer describes? Which does he prefer and why?
He and Madison both describe the Constitution as partly federal. Where do they disagree?
Is there an emergency, as the Federalists said? Compare this letter with Federalist 15.

pieces.t: Letters from the Federal Farmer, II
pieces.au: Signed "The Federal Farmer." For about two centuries the letters were credited to Richard Henry Lee of Virginia, as in Ford's edition used here. Many modern scholars doubt this. Some have argued for Melancton Smith of New York, and more recently some have argued for Elbridge Gerry. The author is still debated.
pieces.desc: Federal Farmer II (dated October 9, 1787): the full text with paragraph numbers, an introduction, key passages and the Federalist reply.
pieces.c: The second letter turns to representation and juries, which the writer calls the essential parts of a free government.
pieces.m: A free government needs "a full and equal representation of the people" and "the jury trial of the vicinage" (local juries). One national government could not provide either over so large a country. He also argues that certain "unalienable and fundamental rights" should be written into the Constitution.

k.q: The essential parts of a free and good government are a full and equal representation of the people in the legislature, and the jury trial of the vicinage
k.w: His two pillars of free government.

k.q: There are certain unalienable and fundamental rights
k.w: His case for a bill of rights.

qs: What does "jury trial of the vicinage" mean? Why does the writer think it matters?
Compare his idea of representation with Hamilton's in Federalist 35.

pieces.t: Letters from the Federal Farmer, III
pieces.au: Signed "The Federal Farmer." For about two centuries the letters were credited to Richard Henry Lee of Virginia, as in Ford's edition used here. Many modern scholars doubt this. Some have argued for Melancton Smith of New York, and more recently some have argued for Elbridge Gerry. The author is still debated.
pieces.desc: Federal Farmer III (dated October 10, 1787): the full text with paragraph numbers, an introduction, key passages and the Federalist reply.
pieces.c: The longest letter, a detailed review of the plan's structure and powers.
pieces.m: The writer argues that the House is too small to represent the people fairly, and that the Senate mixes legislative, executive and judicial powers. He examines the taxing power, the army, the militia and the federal courts, and fears that power will drift to a few men. He grants that the convention faced real limits, but says the result needs amendment.

k.q: the house of representatives, the democrative branch, as it is called, is to consist of 65 members
k.w: His analysis of the small House.

k.q: A power to lay and collect taxes at discretion, is, in itself, of very great importance
k.w: His concern about the taxing power.

k.q: There can be but one supreme court in which the final jurisdiction will centre in all federal causes
k.w: His concern about the courts.

qs: List the parts of the government the writer examines. Which criticism seems strongest to you?
Compare his view of the Senate with Federalist 62 and 63.

pieces.t: Letters from the Federal Farmer, IV
pieces.au: Signed "The Federal Farmer." For about two centuries the letters were credited to Richard Henry Lee of Virginia, as in Ford's edition used here. Many modern scholars doubt this. Some have argued for Melancton Smith of New York, and more recently some have argued for Elbridge Gerry. The author is still debated.
pieces.desc: Federal Farmer IV (dated October 12, 1787): the full text with paragraph numbers, an introduction, key passages and the Federalist reply.
pieces.c: The fourth letter turns to rights and treaties.
pieces.m: Because the Constitution and federal laws will be supreme, the rights protected by state constitutions may not protect people against federal power. The writer argues that the people should state their rights clearly, including freedom of the press, jury trial, protection from unreasonable searches and freedom of religion. He also discusses treaties and the amendment process.

k.q: There are certain rights which we have always held sacred in the United States
k.w: The start of his case for a bill of rights.

k.q: this bill of rights ought to be carried farther
k.w: He says the Constitution's few protections are not enough.

k.q: The trial by jury is very important in another point of view
k.w: Why juries matter for self-government.

qs: Which rights does the writer want written into the Constitution? Compare his list with the Bill of Rights.
How does Hamilton answer this kind of argument in Federalist 84?

pieces.t: Letters from the Federal Farmer, V
pieces.au: Signed "The Federal Farmer." For about two centuries the letters were credited to Richard Henry Lee of Virginia, as in Ford's edition used here. Many modern scholars doubt this. Some have argued for Melancton Smith of New York, and more recently some have argued for Elbridge Gerry. The author is still debated.
pieces.desc: Federal Farmer V (dated October 15, 1787): the full text with paragraph numbers, an introduction, key passages and the Federalist reply.
pieces.c: The last of the original five letters. (An "Additional Number of Letters" followed in 1788 and is not reproduced here.)
pieces.m: The writer sums up: there are good things in the plan, and the states need a stronger federal government, but the plan puts too much power in too few hands. The rational course is to adopt it only with amendments, and he warns against both haste and the pressure of interested men.

k.q: There are, however, in my opinion, many good things in the proposed system
k.w: He gives the plan credit.

k.q: I can discern but one rational mode of proceeding relative to it
k.w: His recommended course: examine freely, state amendments, and adopt them.

qs: What does the writer praise in the plan, and what does he want changed?
Compare his view of amendments with Federalist 85.

pieces.t: George Mason's Objections to the Constitution
pieces.au: By George Mason of Virginia, who wrote the Virginia Declaration of Rights (1776). He was a delegate to the Constitutional Convention and one of three delegates still present at the end who refused to sign. His authorship is not in doubt.
pieces.desc: George Mason's Objections to the Constitution (1787), which open with "There is no declaration of rights": the full text, an introduction and the Federalist reply.
pieces.c: Mason drafted these objections in the last days of the Convention and sent them to George Washington in October 1787. They circulated in manuscript and were printed in newspapers that November. James Iredell of North Carolina answered them in a pamphlet signed "Marcus."
pieces.m: Mason's list is short and pointed: no declaration of rights; a House that is only "the shadow" of representation; a Senate with too much power; federal courts that will absorb the states'; no council for the President; a pardon power that could shield the guilty; commercial laws passed by bare majorities that could hurt the Southern states; a "general clause" that could stretch federal power; and the protection of the slave trade until 1808, which he says weakens the nation. He predicts the government will start as "a moderate aristocracy."

k.q: There is no declaration of rights
k.w: His first and most famous objection.

k.q: there is not the substance, but the shadow only of representation
k.w: His complaint about the House.

k.q: the general legislature is restrained from prohibiting the further importation of slaves for twenty odd years
k.w: Mason, himself a slaveholder, objected to the clause protecting the slave trade.

k.q: This government will commence in a moderate aristocracy
k.w: His prediction.

qs: Which of Mason's objections were answered by the Bill of Rights or later amendments?
Mason wanted a council to advise the President. Read Federalist 70. Why did Hamilton oppose such a council?
Mason objected to the slave-trade clause while himself holding people in slavery. Historians discuss how founders reconciled such positions. What reasons does Mason give in this text?

pieces.t: Observations on the New Constitution, by a Columbian Patriot
pieces.pub: Pamphlet, Boston; reprinted in New York
pieces.au: Published without a name. Ford's 1888 edition, used here, credited Elbridge Gerry. In 1930 the historian Charles Warren showed from letters of the time that it was written by Mercy Otis Warren of Massachusetts, a poet, playwright and later a historian of the Revolution. Her authorship is now accepted.
pieces.desc: Mercy Otis Warren's Observations on the New Constitution (1788), signed "A Columbian Patriot": the full text, an introduction and the Federalist reply.
pieces.c: Massachusetts had ratified narrowly on February 6, 1788, after its convention recommended amendments. Warren's pamphlet appeared that month; the New York Anti-Federalist committee had about 1,630 copies sent out across the state, according to Ford. Warren wrote in a high, literary style that one New York committee thought "too sublime and florid for the common people."
pieces.m: Warren argues that Americans fought for liberty and should not now give it away. She lists eighteen objections: no protection for the rights of conscience or the press; unclear limits on the courts; executive and legislature blended; no civil juries; a standing army; no rotation in office; too few representatives; a Senate that will serve for life; no bill of rights; one government over too large a country; and a convention that exceeded its instructions. She urges amendment before adoption.

k.q: There is no security in the profered system, either for the rights of conscience or the liberty of the Press
k.w: Her second objection.

k.q: There is no provision for a rotation, nor anything to prevent the perpetuity of office in the same hands for life
k.w: Her worry about permanent officeholders.

k.q: There is no provision by a bill of rights to guard against the dangerous encroachments of power
k.w: Her case for a bill of rights.

qs: List five of Warren's eighteen objections. Which were addressed by the Bill of Rights?
Why might the pamphlet first have been credited to a man? What does the later discovery tell us about how historians work?
Warren writes in a high, dramatic style. How does her style differ from Hamilton's or Madison's? Does it help or hurt her argument?

pieces.t: An Address to the People of the State of New York, by a Plebeian
pieces.au: Signed "A Plebeian." Generally attributed to Melancton Smith of New York, a merchant who led the Anti-Federalists at the state's ratifying convention and, in the end, voted to ratify.
pieces.desc: An Address to the People of the State of New York by "A Plebeian" (1788), arguing for amendments before ratification: the full text, an introduction and the Federalist reply.
pieces.c: By spring 1788 several states had ratified, and Federalists argued that it was too late to change the plan. John Jay had just published his own pamphlet, An Address to the People of the State of New York, urging adoption; the Plebeian answers it in a postscript.
pieces.m: The Plebeian says both sides now agree the plan has defects; the only question is whether to amend before adopting or after. He argues that the country is not in such danger that it must accept a flawed plan, that the states will not attack New York for waiting, and that amendments are more likely to be made before adoption than after, when those in power will have no reason to give it up.

k.q: Government is a compact entered into by mankind, in a state of society, for the promotion of their happiness
k.w: His idea of government as a compact.

k.q: I ask, why not amend, and then adopt it?
k.w: The heart of his argument.

k.q: The present is the most important crisis at which you ever have arrived
k.w: His appeal at the close.

qs: What is the Plebeian's main question, and how does Hamilton answer it in Federalist 85?
Melancton Smith, the likely author, finally voted to ratify New York's Constitution. Why might someone who preferred amendments first change his vote? (Look at the ratification timeline.)
Is it easier to change a plan before or after it takes effect? Give an example from your own life or from history.

pieces.series: Patrick Henry in the Virginia convention
pieces.au: Spoken by Patrick Henry. The words come from David Robertson's shorthand record of the debates, published in 1788–89 and reprinted in Elliot's Debates, so they are the reporter's version of what Henry said.
pieces.desc: Patrick Henry's Speech of June 4, 1788, in the Virginia ratifying convention: the full text, an introduction, key passages and the Federalist reply.
pieces.c: Virginia's ratifying convention met in Richmond in June 1788. Patrick Henry, a former governor and the most famous orator of the Revolution, led the opposition. On the convention's third day he gave this short first speech.
pieces.m: Henry asks what danger made the change necessary, and who gave the Convention authority to speak for "We, the people" instead of "We, the states." He says the plan would replace a confederation with a consolidated national government, and that the delegates were sent only to amend the Articles.

k.q: who authorized them to speak the language of, We, the people, instead of, We, the states?
k.w: Henry's famous challenge to the Preamble.

k.q: what danger could have arisen under the present Confederation
k.w: He asks why change is needed at all.

qs: Why does Henry object to the words "We, the people"? How does Madison answer in Federalist 39 and 40?
Henry asks what the danger was. Make the Federalist case from Federalist 15 in two sentences.

pieces.series: Patrick Henry in the Virginia convention
pieces.au: Spoken by Patrick Henry. The words come from David Robertson's shorthand record of the debates, published in 1788–89 and reprinted in Elliot's Debates, so they are the reporter's version of what Henry said.
pieces.desc: Patrick Henry's Speech of June 5, 1788, in the Virginia ratifying convention: the full text, an introduction, key passages and the Federalist reply.
pieces.c: On June 5 Henry spoke for much of the day. This is his longest and most famous speech of the convention. At one point the reporter, David Robertson, summarizes a passage in brackets instead of recording Henry's words.
pieces.m: Henry says liberty, not a powerful empire, should be the aim of American government. He warns that the plan gives up the states' rights, that its amendment process would let a small minority of states block changes, that Congress's control of the militia and a standing army could be used against the people, and that the President could become a king. He asks for strong guarantees of rights and doubts that Virginia faces any danger great enough to justify the risk.

k.q: Guard with jealous attention the public liberty. Suspect every one who approaches that jewel.
k.w: His most quoted line.

k.q: one tenth, or less, of the people of America
k.w: His argument that the amendment process lets a minority block change.

k.q: The first thing I have at heart is American liberty: the second thing is American union
k.w: Henry ranks his priorities.

k.q: it squints towards monarchy
k.w: His view of the presidency.

qs: What does Henry mean when he says the plan "squints towards monarchy"? How does Hamilton answer in Federalists 67 to 70?
Henry ranks liberty above union. How would Madison or Hamilton rank them?
Henry says a small minority could block amendments. Check his math against Article V. Is he right?

pieces.series: Patrick Henry in the Virginia convention
pieces.au: Spoken by Patrick Henry. The words come from David Robertson's shorthand record of the debates, published in 1788–89 and reprinted in Elliot's Debates, so they are the reporter's version of what Henry said.
pieces.desc: Patrick Henry's Speech of June 24, 1788, in the Virginia ratifying convention: the full text, an introduction, key passages and the Federalist reply.
pieces.c: On June 24 the Federalists moved to ratify with recommended amendments, and Henry made one of his last pleas for amendments first. New Hampshire had become the ninth state to ratify on June 21, though the news had not yet reached Richmond. A violent thunderstorm struck as he finished. Virginia ratified the next day, 89 to 79, and recommended a bill of rights and other amendments.
pieces.m: Henry argues that amendments recommended after ratification will never be adopted, because the new government will have no reason to limit itself. He insists that a bill of rights must come first, that nations which trusted to "logical deduction" have lost their liberty, and he warns of the "awful immensity" of the dangers he foresees.

k.q: He asked me where was the power of emancipating slaves
k.w: Henry argues that implied powers could one day reach slavery; this was one reason some Southern delegates opposed the plan.
